Accessibility

If you have dyslexia, try Lexend or OpenDyslexic (under Font) with Wide spacing. What helps differs from person to person, and every change shows straight away, so try a few.

ContrastHigh makes text darker and lines stronger (brighter in dark mode).
Color visionFor color blindness: colors that stay apart for you, in the chapter list (Canon, WIP, Non-canon), the beat families and the colors you give entries.
Text spacingMore room between letters and words, everywhere in the Studio.

About

Story Studio is where your books come together: drafts, the Story bible, canon checks, and the Emotion Beat Bank it grew from. These settings are kept on this device, so your phone can look different from your computer. Sending edits back to Google Drive is the one that follows your account.

What each one does
Continue writing
Claude writes what comes next, in your voice: two versions to pick from, or your selected notes made into prose.
Rewrite selection
Select a line or a paragraph first: Claude gives you other ways to say it.
Suggest edits
Claude marks changes in your text for you to accept or dismiss, one by one or all at once. Nothing changes until you do. Select part of the chapter first to do only that part.
Grammar & typos
Fixes slips in spelling, grammar and punctuation. Your style and voice stay.
Show, don’t tell
Finds feelings you’ve named (“she was scared”) and suggests what the body does instead.
Cut extra words
Finds wordy lines and suggests shorter ones that say the same thing.
Sharpen wording
Suggests stronger, more specific words for lines that fall flat.
Italics & bold
Where italics or bold belong (thoughts, stress, titles, other languages), each with why.
Story bible
Flags anything in the chapter that contradicts your Story bible.
Canon check ↗
Opens Canon check with this chapter, to check it against the chapters before it.
Bible additions ↗
Finds names, places and details your Story bible doesn’t have yet.
Reader pass
How it reads to a reader: where it grips, drags or confuses. Changes nothing.
Posting kit
A rating, warnings, tags and summaries for posting it.
Toned-down copy
A copy with the explicit parts toned down, saved as a new draft.
Example passage. Tap a highlight to see what the checks found, then bring your own writing.

    Chapters and drafts

    Plotlines

    The main plot, each character’s arc, the romances and the subplots, and the chapters each one moves in, as Claude reads them. Add a thread of your own and say what it’s about: Claude finds it in the chapters.

    Pacing map

    How fast each chapter reads, and what goes into it: physical action, how much story time passes, urgency and stakes, how close the telling sits to the point-of-view character, and how much of it is dialogue. Plot points come from the plotlines.

    Canon check

    Test a WIP draft, a non-canon scene or something someone shared with you against what’s already canon: what it contradicts, what it would change, what’s new, and which chapters would need another look.

    Show, don’t tell — a phrase bank for fiction

    Emotion Beat Bank

    Body-language beats for 40 emotions and 17 states of the body, like pain and sickness, using magic and fighting: three intensities each, five places the body gives it away, and the tells that leak out when a character tries to hide it. Switch the point of view and every line rewrites itself. Tap any line to copy it.

      • Outside view: what others see, not what the character feels
      • Hiding it: tells that leak past a mask
      • / jumps to search
      Order

      Order

      Nothing matches “” with the current filters.

      Try a synonym (“nervous” finds Anxiety, “bored” finds Boredom), or .

      Overused tells

      Beats readers have seen so often they skim right past them. Each comes with three fresher swaps, rewritten in your chosen point of view.

      Romance & spice

      Craft notes

      How to use a bank like this without your prose starting to sound like one.

      One beat is usually enough

      Stack three tells on one line of dialogue and none of them land. Pick the one that fits this character in this moment, and trust it.

      Climb the intensity

      Start a scene at Low and let it build. A character who opens at Devastated has nowhere left to go.

      Subtext lives in the gap

      The “Hiding it” rows are where tension comes from: a steady voice over shaking hands. Readers love catching what a character won’t say.

      Rotate the body

      If your last three beats were faces, reach for hands, posture or breath. Filter by body area to find one fast.

      Mind the point of view

      Lines marked show how a character looks from outside. A first-person or deep-POV narrator can’t see their own pallor or pupils, so write what it feels like instead, or give the line to someone watching.

      Give characters a signature

      A ring they turn, a sleeve they tug. Repeat one habit across the book and readers learn to read it without being told. Pick a character up top and tap ☆ on the beats that fit them: they gather at the top of each emotion.

      Let beats do the tagging

      An action beat can replace “he said” and show emotion at the same time. If the dialogue already says it, cut the beat.

      Make it yours

      The props here are placeholders. Swap in your world (the cup becomes a tankard, the map a star chart) so the line sounds like your book, not a list.

      For spicy scenes

      Consent reads as heat

      Enthusiastic cues (pulling closer, meeting the kiss, a breathless yes) make a scene hotter, not slower. Let bodies ask and answer.

      Slow the camera down

      Intimate scenes stretch time. A single button, a held breath or a hand that hesitates can carry more heat than a paragraph of action.

      Keep the people in the room

      The best spicy scenes are character scenes. Let nerves, humor and tenderness surface between the heat, so the scene could only belong to these characters.

      Set the heat with words

      These beats work at any spice level. How explicit you go is a choice of vocabulary layered on top of the same body language.

      Past tense throughout. Point of view, character, order and filters are remembered on this device; the beats you tag for a character are saved with them in your story bible.

      Story bible

      Characters, world terms and style rules. The AI tools follow them, and the editor’s Story bible check flags anything in a draft that contradicts them.

      Characters

      Suggested additions

      Claude reads your chapters for the names, places, things, groups and events your Story bible doesn’t have yet, and files each one where it fits best. It also spots new details for entries you already have, like a new scar or a new relationship. Nothing goes in until you add it, and non-canon chapters, like alternate timelines, are only read when you pick them.

      Documents

      Worldbuilding documents brought into the Story bible. Claude sorts each one into entries, keeping your words and leaving out the template’s questions and notes, and adds to entries you already have. Open one to see everything it added, or to read it again once it’s changed.

      Bringing in a document needs Claude, which isn’t available here right now.

      No documents yet. Bring one in from Google Drive, or paste one, and it’s listed here with a link back to it.
